CHAPTER 3.2 · LEARNING AREA 3

CHAPTER 3.2 · LEARNING AREA 3 · SEPTEMBER

The definite integral and the fundamental theorem

A water meter only knows the rate of flow, a speedometer only the speed. How much water is in the tank and how far the car has travelled lies in the area under the graph of the rate. You approximate this area with strips, get to know the definite integral as their limit and calculate it with the fundamental theorem of calculus, without any strips at all.

10 LESSONS3 UNITS4 WIDGETS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • reconstruct the total from a rate of change and interpret the result as an area
  • approximate areas with lower and upper sums and understand the definite integral as a limit
  • calculate with the signed area and the properties of the integral
  • apply the fundamental theorem and recognise the integral function as an antiderivative
  • prove the fundamental theorem, interpret the graph of an integral function and read integrals as physical quantities

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Total from rates of change, upper and lower sums

If 3 litres per minute flow in for 8 minutes, $3 \cdot 8 = 24$ litres are added: exactly the area of the rectangle under the graph of the rate. If the rate changes, you split the time into short intervals in which it is almost constant. Each interval gives a narrow rectangle, and together they make up almost the area under the graph.

This holds for every rate of change: from the speed you get the distance, from the power the energy, from the rate of inflow the amount of water. If the rate is negative, the total decreases. Pieces of area below the axis therefore count as negative: this is called the signed area.

To pin down the area, you take the smallest function value in each strip (lower sum $L_n$) and the largest (upper sum $U_n$). The area lies between them. As the strips get narrower and narrower, both sums approach the same limit, the definite integral.

KEY POINT · THE DEFINITE INTEGRAL

If the lower and upper sums of $f$ on $[a, b]$ have the same limit for $n \to \infty$, it is called the definite integral: $$\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \lim_{n \to \infty} L_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} U_n$$

It is a signed area: parts above the $x$-axis count as positive, parts below as negative.

Reconstructed total: if $r$ is the rate of change of $B$, then $\displaystyle B(b) = B(a) + \int_a^b r(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Units: rate times time. Litres per minute times minutes gives litres, metres per second times seconds gives metres.

The names $a$ and $b$ are the lower and upper limits of integration, $f$ is the integrand.

INTERACTIVE · THE TOTAL FROM THE RATE

At the top the rate, at the bottom the total. Move the time on: the area under the rate up to that moment is exactly the change in the total. Where the rate becomes negative, the total goes down.

INTERACTIVE · LOWER SUM AND UPPER SUM

Green the lower sum, red on top of it what the upper sum has in addition. Increase the number of strips and watch the red remainder disappear.

EXAMPLE 1 · TOO SMALL AND TOO LARGE

Pin down $\int_0^2 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x$ with four strips of width 0.5.

$x^2$ increases on $[0, 2]$: in every strip the smallest value is on the left, the largest on the right.

$L_4 = 0.5 \cdot (0 + 0.25 + 1 + 2.25) = 1.75$, $U_4 = 0.5 \cdot (0.25 + 1 + 2.25 + 4) = 3.75$: $1.75 \le \int_0^2 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le 3.75$

EXAMPLE 2 · WATER LEVEL

A tank holds 20 l. For four minutes 2 l/min flow in, after that the rate falls steadily according to $r(t) = 6 - t$ until $t = 8$. How much water is in the tank after 4, 6 and 8 minutes?

Up to $t = 4$: rectangle $2 \cdot 4 = 8$, so 28 l. From 4 to 6: triangle $\tfrac12 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 2$, so 30 l.

From 6 to 8, $r < 0$: a triangle below the axis, −2. 28 l, 30 l, 28 l; the tank holds the most water at $t = 6$.

EXERCISES

A car drives at 15 m/s for 10 s and then at 25 m/s for 20 s. Draw the $v$-$t$ diagram and find the distance.

Two rectangles: $150 + 500 = 650$ m

The inflow into a pool grows steadily according to $r(t) = 0.5t$ (in l/min). How much water flows in during the first 10 minutes?

Triangle: $\tfrac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 5 = 25$ l

Calculate the lower and upper sums of $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1]$ with four strips. Where is the integral?

$L_4 = 0.25 \cdot (0 + 0.25 + 0.5 + 0.75) = 0.375$, $U_4 = 0.625$. The integral $\tfrac12$ (triangle) lies exactly in the middle.

An open-air pool opens at 9 am. Until 12 noon, 200 more visitors arrive than leave every hour. From 12 noon to 3 pm arrivals and departures balance out, from 3 pm to 7 pm 150 more visitors leave than arrive every hour. How many visitors are in the pool at 12 noon, 3 pm and 7 pm?

600, 600, $600 - 4 \cdot 150 = 0$: at 7 pm the pool is empty.

For $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ with $n$ strips, $L_n = \dfrac{(n - 1)\,n\,(2n - 1)}{6n^3}$ and $U_n = \dfrac{n\,(n + 1)\,(2n + 1)}{6n^3}$. Calculate $L_{10}$ and $U_{10}$ and find the common limit.

For the limit, divide numerator and denominator by $n^3$.

$L_{10} = \tfrac{9 \cdot 10 \cdot 19}{6000} = 0.285$, $U_{10} = \tfrac{10 \cdot 11 \cdot 21}{6000} = 0.385$. For $n \to \infty$ both tend to $\tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac13$: $\int_0^1 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac13$.

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Properties of the integral and the fundamental theorem

With the inflow $r(t) = 0.5t$, 25 litres were added in ten minutes. $R(t) = 0.25t^2$ is an antiderivative of $r$, and $R(10) - R(0) = 25$. Coincidence? No: the area under a graph can always be read off from an antiderivative.

The reason lies in the integral function $I_a(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$, the area from $a$ up to the variable limit $x$. If you move $x$ on by a small amount $h$, a narrow strip is added, almost a rectangle with the area $f(x) \cdot h$. So the area grows at the rate $f(x)$: $I_a'(x) = f(x)$. The integral function is an antiderivative, and every other one differs from it only by a constant. In $F(b) - F(a)$ this constant drops out.

KEY POINT · FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS

If $F$ is any antiderivative of the continuous function $f$, then $$\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \Big[F(x)\Big]_a^b = F(b) - F(a)$$

Integral function: $I_a(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$ is an antiderivative of $f$ with $I_a(a) = 0$.

Properties: $\int_a^a f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0$ · $\int_a^b f + \int_b^c f = \int_a^c f$ · $\int_b^a f = -\int_a^b f$ · $\int_a^b (k f + g) = k\int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$

Two sides of the same coin: differentiating and integrating undo each other. That is what makes the fundamental theorem so powerful: instead of adding up strips, you look for an antiderivative.

On the CAS you enter the integrand, the variable and both limits. The variable of integration can have any name: $\int_0^2 t^2\,\mathrm{d}t = \int_0^2 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x$.

INTERACTIVE · SIGNED AREA BETWEEN THE LIMITS

Drag the limits $a$ and $b$. Yellow pieces lie above the axis and count as positive, red ones below it count as negative. Compare the integral with the sum of the pieces of area.

EXAMPLE 3 · WITH THE FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM

Calculate $\int_1^3 (x^2 - 2x + 2)\,\mathrm{d}x$.

Antiderivative $F(x) = \tfrac13 x^3 - x^2 + 2x$: $F(3) = 9 - 9 + 6 = 6$, $F(1) = \tfrac13 - 1 + 2 = \tfrac43$.

$6 - \tfrac43 = \tfrac{14}{3} \approx 4.67$

EXAMPLE 4 · AN INTEGRAL FUNCTION

Find $I_0(x) = \int_0^x (2t - 2)\,\mathrm{d}t$. Where is $I_0(x) = 0$, and what does that mean?

$I_0(x) = \left[t^2 - 2t\right]_0^x = x^2 - 2x$, check $I_0'(x) = 2x - 2$ ✔. Zero at $x = 0$ and $x = 2$.

At $x = 2$ the piece below the axis ($[0, 1]$) and the piece above it ($[1, 2]$) cancel out.

EXERCISES

Calculate: a) $\int_1^3 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$   b) $\int_0^1 (3x^2 + 1)\,\mathrm{d}x$   c) $\int_0^\pi \sin x\,\mathrm{d}x$

a) $9 - 1 = 8$   b) $[x^3 + x]_0^1 = 2$   c) $[-\cos x]_0^\pi = 1 + 1 = 2$

Calculate $\int_0^4 (4 - x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ and check the result with the area of a triangle.

$\left[4x - \tfrac12 x^2\right]_0^4 = 16 - 8 = 8$, triangle $\tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 8$ ✔

We know $\int_0^2 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 3$ and $\int_2^5 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = -1$. Find a) $\int_0^5 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$   b) $\int_5^0 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$   c) $\int_0^2 3f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$

a) 2 (additivity over intervals)   b) −2 (limits swapped)   c) 9 (constant multiple rule)

Water flows into a tank holding 20 l at the rate $r(t) = -0.5t^2 + 3t$ (in l/min). How much water is in the tank after 6 and after 9 minutes? When is it fullest?

$R(t) = -\tfrac16 t^3 + 1.5t^2$: $R(6) = 18$, $R(9) = 0$. So 38 l and 20 l again. Fullest at $t = 6$, where $r$ changes sign.

Let $I_0(x) = \int_0^x (t^2 - 4)\,\mathrm{d}t$ for $x \ge 0$. Find $I_0$, its turning point and its positive zero. Interpret the zero as a balance of areas.

$I_0(x) = \tfrac13 x^3 - 4x$. $I_0' = x^2 - 4 = 0$: minimum at $x = 2$. $\tfrac13 x^3 = 4x$ gives $x = \sqrt{12} \approx 3.46$: up to there the piece above the axis ($[2, \sqrt{12}]$) is as large as the piece below it ($[0, 2]$).

TEST YOURSELF!

Calculate $\int_0^2 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x$.

$\tfrac83$

Calculate $\int_1^3 (x^2 - 2x + 2)\,\mathrm{d}x$.

$6 - \tfrac43$

From $a$ to $a$ there is no area.

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3The integral function, a proof and physical quantities

In unit 2 a narrow strip, “almost a rectangle”, was added. In the advanced course we turn this into a proof. You only need two things: a strip always lies between the smallest and the largest rectangle that fits it, and a continuous function hardly changes on a tiny interval.

The integral function $I_a$ also has a graph of its own, which you can read off from the graph of $f$: it has a zero at $a$, it increases where $f$ is positive, has turning points where $f$ changes sign, and points of inflection at the turning points of $f$. Finally, integrals are not just areas: if a rate is integrated over time or a force over distance, you get physical quantities such as distance, charge or work.

KEY POINT · PROOF OF THE FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM

Let $f$ be continuous, $h > 0$ small, $m_h$ and $M_h$ the minimum and the maximum of $f$ on $[x, x + h]$. The strip lies between the rectangles: $$m_h \cdot h \le I_a(x + h) - I_a(x) = \int_x^{x+h} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \le M_h \cdot h$$

Divide by $h$: $m_h \le \dfrac{I_a(x + h) - I_a(x)}{h} \le M_h$. For $h \to 0$, $m_h$ and $M_h$ tend to $f(x)$, because $f$ is continuous. So $I_a'(x) = f(x)$ (likewise for $h < 0$).

If $F$ is any antiderivative, then $F = I_a + C$, and $\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = I_a(b) = F(b) - F(a)$. ∎

Why continuous? At a jump the integral function has a kink. It is not differentiable there, and $I_a' = f$ does not hold at that point.

Physics: distance $s = \int v\,\mathrm{d}t$ · charge $Q = \int I\,\mathrm{d}t$ · work $W = \int F\,\mathrm{d}s$. The unit of the integral is the unit of the integrand times the unit of the variable.

INTERACTIVE · THE INTEGRAL FUNCTION

Drag the yellow point on the $x$-axis. At the top the area from $a$ to $x$ grows, at the bottom the graph of $I_a$ appears point by point. The pink tangent always has the gradient $f(x)$.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE GRAPH OF THE INTEGRAL FUNCTION

$f(x) = x^2 - 2x$, $I_0(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$. Find the zeros, turning points and points of inflection of $I_0$.

$I_0(x) = \tfrac13 x^3 - x^2 = x^2\left(\tfrac13 x - 1\right)$: zeros 0 and 3. $I_0' = f = x(x - 2)$: maximum at 0, minimum at 2 with $I_0(2) = -\tfrac43$.

$I_0'' = f' = 2x - 2$: point of inflection at $x = 1$, the minimum of $f$.

EXAMPLE 6 · WORK ON A SPRING

A spring with the spring constant $D = 200$ N/m is stretched by 10 cm from its rest position. The force grows according to Hooke's law: $F(s) = D \cdot s$. How much work is needed?

$W = \int_0^{0.1} 200\,s\,\mathrm{d}s = \left[100\,s^2\right]_0^{0.1} = 1$ N·m.

$W = 1$ J, in general $W = \tfrac12 D s^2$. A product “force times distance” is not enough, because the force is not constant.

EXERCISES

Write the integral function $I_1(x) = \int_1^x 3t^2\,\mathrm{d}t$ without an integral sign and confirm $I_1(1) = 0$ and $I_1' = 3x^2$.

$I_1(x) = x^3 - 1$, $I_1(1) = 0$, $I_1'(x) = 3x^2$ ✔

A battery is charged with the current $I(t) = 2 - 0.2t$ (in A, $t$ in h) until the current is zero. How much charge flows?

$I(t) = 0$ at $t = 10$: $Q = \int_0^{10} (2 - 0.2t)\,\mathrm{d}t = 20 - 10 = 10$ Ah.

Is every antiderivative also an integral function? Investigate $F(x) = x^2 + 1$ as an antiderivative of $f(x) = 2x$.

No. $I_a(x) = x^2 - a^2$ always has a zero at $a$. $x^2 + 1$ has no zero, so it is not an integral function of $2x$.

The gravitational force on a satellite of mass $m$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth is $F(r) = \dfrac{G M m}{r^2}$. How much work is needed to lift it from the Earth's radius $R$ to $2R$, and how much to take it “infinitely far” away?

For the second question: insert the limit $b$ and consider $b \to \infty$.

$W = \int_R^{2R} \tfrac{GMm}{r^2}\,\mathrm{d}r = GMm\left[-\tfrac1r\right]_R^{2R} = \tfrac{GMm}{2R}$. Up to $b$: $GMm\left(\tfrac1R - \tfrac1b\right) \to \tfrac{GMm}{R}$, so only twice as much. The escape velocity follows from this.

TEST YOURSELF!

$I_0(x) = \int_0^x (t^2 - 2t)\,\mathrm{d}t$: value at the minimum $x = 2$?

$\tfrac83 - 4$

Work in joules to stretch a spring with $D = 200$ N/m by 0.1 m?

$\tfrac12 \cdot 200 \cdot 0.01$

Where does the integral function $I_a$ have its points of inflection?

$I_a'' = f'$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Explain without calculating why $\int_{-1}^{1} (x^3 + x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0$.

The graph has point symmetry about the origin: the piece below the axis on the left is as large as the piece above it on the right.

Connecting with physics: a car brakes with $v(t) = 20 - 4t$ (in m/s) until it stops. How long is the braking distance?

Stops at $t = 5$: $\int_0^5 (20 - 4t)\,\mathrm{d}t = \left[20t - 2t^2\right]_0^5 = 50$ m

Explain: for an increasing function the lower sum is the sum with the left rectangles. What holds for a decreasing function?

Increasing: the left edge of each strip has the smallest value. Decreasing: the largest value is there, so the left rectangles form the upper sum.

Connecting with economics: a business knows its marginal cost $K'(x) = 0.03x^2 - 1.2x + 20$ (in € per unit) and its fixed costs of €500. Find the cost function $K$ and the costs for 40 units. What does $\int_{20}^{40} K'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ mean?

$K$ is the antiderivative of $K'$ with $K(0) = 500$.

$K(x) = 0.01x^3 - 0.6x^2 + 20x + 500$, $K(40) = 640 - 960 + 800 + 500 = 980$, so €980.

$\int_{20}^{40} K'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = K(40) - K(20) = 980 - 740 = 240$: this is how much units 21 to 40 cost in addition.

For which $b > 0$ is $\int_0^b (6 - 2x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 8$? Explain why there are two solutions.

$6b - b^2 = 8$, so $b^2 - 6b + 8 = 0$: $b = 2$ or $b = 4$. From $x = 3$ on the integrand is negative: between 3 and 4 a piece below the axis is added, which exactly cancels the piece between 2 and 3.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Bernhard Riemann and the strips

Newton and Leibniz could calculate with integrals, but what exactly an integral is remained unclear for a long time. For which functions do the sums of strips really approach a fixed value? Bernhard Riemann (17 September 1826 – 20 July 1866) answered this question in his habilitation thesis in Göttingen. It was actually about when a function can be represented by trigonometric series. Along the way he defined what we now call the Riemann integral and gave conditions under which a function is integrable.

In his honour, upper and lower sums like the ones you use in this chapter are also called Riemann sums. Riemann also became famous for his habilitation lecture of 1854 on the foundations of geometry. His ideas about the geometry of curved spaces have deeply shaped modern theoretical physics. Riemann lived to be only 39.

Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: biography “Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann”.
